This integrated approach will enable a mechanistic understanding of how structural transitions within the ice matrix influence its sublimation behavior under varying temperature conditions relevant to the outer Solar System.

We hypothesize that by employing a custom-built ultra-high vacuum cryostat system, integrating in-situ quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) measurements with high temporal resolution, and time-of-flight mass spectrometry (TOF-MS) with velocity map imaging (VMI) capabilities, we can elucidate the non-equilibrium sublimation kinetics of nitrogen, carbon monoxide, and methane ices at temperatures relevant to the outer Solar System (30-80 K). Specifically, by systematically varying the substrate temperature (in fine increments of 2 K) and deposition rate (spanning the range from diffusion-limited to reaction-limited growth), we will quantify the impact of initial ice morphology and defect density on the instantaneous sublimation flux and the translational energy distribution of the desorbing molecules. We predict that for freshly deposited films, particularly at higher deposition rates and lower substrate temperatures, the initial sublimation rate will significantly deviate from predictions based on established equilibrium vapor pressure curves, exhibiting an enhanced flux characterized by a non-Maxwellian translational energy distribution indicative of surface-mediated desorption processes from metastable amorphous regions. Furthermore, by comparing our experimentally determined vapor pressures and latent heats of sublimation with those derived from commonly used empirical relations (e.g., Antoine, Clausius-Clapeyron with astrophysical parameterizations), we anticipate significant discrepancies, especially for methane at the lower end of our temperature range. These discrepancies will be directly correlated with the observed deviations in the translational energy distributions, providing mechanistic insights into the limitations of equilibrium-based models in describing the sublimation of volatile ices under astrophysically relevant non-equilibrium conditions. This approach will not only yield more accurate vapor pressure data but also reveal the kinetic pathways and energy partitioning during sublimation, ultimately refining our understanding of volatile transport and atmospheric evolution on outer Solar System bodies.

The vapor pressures and latent heats of sublimation for volatile ices such as nitrogen, carbon monoxide, and methane at temperatures relevant to the outer Solar System exhibit distinct sublimation behaviors dependent on initial deposition conditions and phase transitions. Specifically, the sublimation rates of freshly deposited amorphous films of these ices, measured using infrared spectroscopy at wavelengths of 3 μm and 10 μm and a quartz crystal microbalance with a resonant frequency of 6 MHz, will show an initial enhancement followed by a decay over time. This behavior will be influenced by the deposition rate within the range of 0.1 to 5 μm/h, substrate temperatures between 30 K and 120 K, and initial film thicknesses ranging from 10 nm to 1 μm. The transformation from amorphous to crystalline phases will occur with an estimated activation energy of 0.44 ± 0.04 eV, and the presence of trace contaminants (such as CO2 and CH4) will alter the sublimation kinetics, providing insights into the role of impurities in phase transition dynamics.

This approach will utilize a step-by-step integration process where spectroscopic data are meticulously calibrated and input into thermodynamic models such as the lattice Boltzmann method and Monte Carlo simulations. Validation will be conducted through comparison metrics with existing data, pilot studies demonstrating feasibility, and error analysis frameworks to account for uncertainties.

The sublimation of volatile ices (nitrogen, carbon monoxide, and methane) at low temperatures exhibits a bi-phasic behavior, characterized by a rapidly sublimating, amorphous-like surface layer overlying a more stable, crystalline-like bulk phase. This bi-phasic behavior can be accurately measured and modeled using Temperature Programmed Desorption (TPD) with a deconvolution analysis employing a sum of a Gaussian function and an Arrhenius function, where the former represent the initial, fast sublimation of the amorphous-like layer and the latter the slower sublimation of the crystalline bulk. Specifically, films of these ices, approximately 1000 monolayers thick, will be deposited onto a temperature-controlled substrate at 10 K using a calibrated deposition rate of 1 monolayer/s. Film thickness will be estimated via a quartz crystal microbalance (QCM), and the 1000 monolayer thickness is measured when the QCM shows the corresponding changes.  Subsequently, temperature-programmed desorption will be performed within an ultra-high vacuum environment (base pressure < 1e-9 mbar). The substrate temperature will be ramped at a rate of 0.1 K/s from 10 K to 80 K, and the partial pressures of the sublimated species will be monitored using a mass spectrometer (Quadrupole mass spectrometer, with a mass range of 1-100 amu and a sensitivity of at least 1e-12 mbar). The data will be collected using LabVIEW interface at a sampling rate of 10 Hz, which is greater than the response rate of the mass spectrometer and can provide sufficient time resolution. We will use a custom-made cold finger to deposit the samples at low temperature, with temperature regulated via a Lakeshore 336 temperature controller with an accuracy of 0.1 K.  The TPD profile will be fitted by a sum of two functions:
    1.  A Gaussian function, defined as  $G(T) = A \cdot exp(-\frac{(T-T_p)^2}{2 \sigma^2})$, where A represents the peak amplitude, T_p is the peak temperature, and  σ represents the width of the peak, representing the sublimation of the amorphous-like surface layer.
    2. An Arrhenius function, defined as $R(T) = \nu \cdot exp(-\frac{E_a}{k_B T})$, where $E_a$ is the activation energy for sublimation of crystalline-like ice,  ν is the pre-exponential factor and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.  The overall fitting function is a sum of these two functions, $f(T) = G(T) + R(T)$.  The uncertainties of the parameters will be estimated from the fitting routine and represent the fitting precision on the fitted parameters.

     The activation energy $E_a$ can be directly extracted from the Arrhenius function. The effective vapor pressure for the crystalline phase will be calculated from the extracted value of the Arrhenius pre-factor $\nu$ and the activation energy $E_a$ by applying the transition state theory.

   The integrated area under the Gaussian curve, proportional to A  σ, will be used to calculate the relative thickness of the amorphous-like surface layer. This area will be correlated with the substrate temperature during deposition. Specifically, we hypothesize a positive correlation between the relative thickness of the amorphous-like surface layer and deposition at 10K. This correlation will be quantified using linear regression or an equivalent, based on the obtained data, model. To support this hypothesis, additional experiments will be performed with deposition of the same ices at 60K using a slow deposition rate (0.1 monolayer/s) to promote crystallinity during deposition.  We hypothesize that deposition at 60 K will result in a reduced area under the Gaussian curve, and thus a thinner amorphous-like surface layer, compared to deposition at 10K, if the growth conditions are responsible for the observed two phases.  Furthermore, to study the structural transformation from the amorphous-like to crystalline-like phase, the as-deposited film will be annealed at intermediate temperatures (between 20 K and 50K) for 15 minutes. The TPD curves of these annealed samples will be collected. The annealing induced thickness reduction of the amorphous-like surface layer will be measured from a reduced integrated Gaussian part of the deconvolved TPD profile. This effect will also be compared for the differently deposited samples. To verify that the measured rate is in the kinetic regime, we will conduct additional TPD measurements, by systematically varying the heating rate by a factor of two, 0.05 K/s and 0.2 K/s. We will be monitoring the shift in peak temperature of both the Gaussian peak and the Arrhenius peak (if detectable) at these different heating rates. This shift can be used to verify whether the sublimation is in the kinetic regime based on a Redhead Analysis, which relates the peak temperature to the heating rate, and verifies that the sublimation rate is a function of the sample temperature alone, which indicates that we are in the kinetic regime.  Specifically, we expect that the amorphous-like peak will shift to higher temperatures with a higher heating rate, and it follows the Redhead analysis: ln(β/Tp2) = -Ea/(RTp) + ln(νR/Ea) where β is the heating rate, R is the universal gas constant, and Ea is the activation energy. This is the first time TPD is applied to study the bi-phasic sublimation behavior of these volatile ices with a dual function deconvolution of the TPD curve and a quantitative analysis of the amorphous surface layer and the evolution of this layer upon temperature increase.  The effective activation energy and pre-exponential factor from the Arrhenius fitting of the low-temperature regime can be compared with existing literature to determine whether the sublimation behavior of our prepared films follows the same rule as in the previous studies. With our quantitative analysis, we can get a better understanding of the activation energies, and the stability of the amorphous and crystalline phases of these volatile ices. The bi-phasic sublimation model can significantly improve the interpretation of astronomical observations, especially in outer Solar System objects, where volatile ices are abundant. For instance, the surface composition, as well as the effective vapor pressure of icy objects can be modeled with more accuracy based on the bi-phasic sublimation model. This new understanding will allow the community to have a better understanding of the surface evolution of these icy bodies. This method could be adapted to study other types of volatile ices, such as water ice or other organic molecules. The results could also be used in industrial applications, where understanding of the sublimation processes is required.

We hypothesize that an iteratively refined hybrid thermodynamic-experimental approach, leveraging high-accuracy vapor pressure relationships from the bibliographic review as a starting point and integrating targeted, high-precision measurements of both vapor pressure and latent heat of sublimation at strategically selected low temperatures, will yield significantly more accurate and physically consistent predictions of vapor pressures and latent heats of sublimation for nitrogen, carbon monoxide, and methane in astrophysically relevant cold environments compared to purely empirical extrapolations, sole reliance on the reviewed thermodynamic formulae, or single-point experimental anchoring. Specifically, this approach will involve: (1) Initializing vapor pressure predictions using the most accurate thermodynamic relations identified in the bibliographic review for each ice species. (2) Conducting precise experimental measurements of both vapor pressure (using capacitance manometry with in-situ calibration) and latent heat of sublimation (using adiabatic calorimetry) at a minimal number of strategically chosen temperatures close to the expected condensation temperatures in outer Solar System environments (e.g., 30-50 K for N₂, 20-40 K for CO, and 10-30 K for CH₄). These temperatures will be selected to maximize sensitivity to deviations in the thermodynamic predictions and to span key temperature regimes relevant to specific astrophysical bodies. (3) Employing the experimental vapor pressure data to iteratively refine parameters within the selected thermodynamic equations from the review, focusing on parameters with the highest sensitivity at the measured temperatures (e.g., enthalpy and entropy of sublimation). This refinement will be achieved through a non-linear least squares fitting procedure, weighted by the uncertainties of both the experimental data and the original thermodynamic relations. (4) Validating the refined vapor pressure curves by comparing predictions to independent, high-accuracy experimental data points where available, and assessing the thermodynamic consistency between the refined vapor pressure curves and the experimentally determined latent heats of sublimation using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. Significant improvement will be defined by a statistically significant reduction in the residuals between predicted and experimental values, and a demonstrable improvement in the internal thermodynamic consistency of the derived vapor pressure and latent heat data compared to existing relations. This targeted experimental validation and iterative refinement of existing thermodynamic frameworks, grounded in the comprehensive bibliographic review, will provide a more physically robust and accurate method for determining these crucial thermophysical properties at astrophysically relevant conditions.
